TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
MONDAY, 27 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 10:03 AM (AEST)
DAY 37
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY, KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MS KATRINA MUSGROVE, for the Commonwealth
MS JENNIFER FINDLAY, for Mr Mark Wood

COMMISSIONER: Yes. Appearances, please?
MR SCOTT: May it please, Commissioner, I appear with Ms Marsh this morning.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: May it please the Commission, I appear today with Ms Katrina
Musgrove for the Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And we have another appearance too?
MS FINDLAY: May it please the Commission. My name is Findlay. I appear for Mark Wood.
COMMISSIONER: For Mark Wood. Ms Findlay, I don't know if you have any interest in the
witnesses who will be called this morning, who I think are Mr Gladman, Ms Carmody and
Ms Kruse?
MS FINDLAY: I don't think so.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Well, can we give Ms Findlay a time estimate?
MR SCOTT: I think an hour and a half for these three witnesses, but there is a mention of
Mr Wood in some of the emails that came through overnight. So perhaps Ms Findlay might
have an interest.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I might be able to assist. There has been two
Supplementary Statements for two witnesses this morning. At least one of those includes
material that would be relevant to Mr Wood's interests.
COMMISSIONER: It looks as if you're stuck here, Ms Findlay.
MS FINDLAY: Thank you. I will do so.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks. Yes. So you are calling Mr Gladman?
MR SCOTT: I do. But before I do, can I tender some but not all of the exhibits in the list for
today. Those are the exhibits commencing on Exhibit 5806 and ending with Exhibit 5938.
That's the exhibits that relate to the first three witnesses of the day, Commissioner.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: And, Commissioner, could I foreshadow that I understand my friend
may need to additionally tender the documents that are related to Exhibit 5810A, which is
the Supplementary Statement of Ms Kruse, which has only been provided to the Commission
overnight, and I believe he has not yet had an opportunity to see the documents that are
referred to in that.

COMMISSIONER: Up to you –
MR SCOTT: Pardon, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: You may need to tender other documents, I gather, which - I'm just
checking this. Yes, the Supplementary Statement of Ms Kruse.
MR SCOTT: Yes, there is, as I understand, about six additional documents which are referred
to in that Statement, which we are just waiting on production of them from the
Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: You don't actually have them yet?
MR SCOTT: No.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Alright. So it is 5806 through to 5938, I think. Is that correct?
MR SCOTT: Yes, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Those documents are admitted and marked with the numbers they
bear in the exhibit list.
<EXHIBITS 5806 TO 5938 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
COMMISSIONER: And, Mr Gladman, will you take an oath or an affirmation?
MR GLADMAN: An affirmation, please.
COMMISSIONER: Right. Would you stand, please?
<MARK STANLEY GLADMAN, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Thank you Commissioner. Mr Gladman, would you please inform the Commission
of your full name?
MR GLADMAN: Mark Stanley Gladman.
MR SCOTT: And you were provided a Notice to Give Information in Writing and Produce
Documents from the Commission dated the 6th of January 2023?
MR GLADMAN: That's correct.

MR SCOTT: And you produced a Statement in response to that Notice dated the 30th of
January 2023?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you have also produced a Supplementary Statement dated the 26th of
February 2023?
MR GLADMAN: I did.
MR SCOTT: Are the contents of your Statements true and correct to the best of your
knowledge and belief?
MR GLADMAN: They are.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. You are currently working as a lawyer; correct?
MR GLADMAN: I retired last week.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I was reading from your first Statement, so that's - - -
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: - - - why, it's out of date. But until recently, you were working as a lawyer?
MR GLADMAN: Until last Thursday, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. Is this right: in January 2016, you commenced work at the
Department of Human Services in the role of Deputy General Counsel, Program Advice and
Privacy Branch?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: You held this role until the 7th of December 2018?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And from December 2016 to January 2017, you held the role of Acting General
Counsel, Program Advice and Privacy Branch?
MR GLADMAN: Sorry, what was the dates? There was a four-week period late December to
early January. Is that the - sorry, could you repeat the question?
MR SCOTT: From December 2016 - - -
MR GLADMAN: Yes.

MR SCOTT: - - - to January 2017, you held the role of Acting General Counsel, Program Advice
and Privacy Branch - - -
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: - - - for about a period of four weeks?
MR GLADMAN: About four weeks, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. And that period included the first couple of weeks of January
2017?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. Now, you've got a reasonably large folder in front of you,
Mr Gladman. The documents that I will be asking you questions about are contained in that
folder. They will also be coming up on the screen.
MR GLADMAN: Sure.
MR SCOTT: The first document I want to ask you a question about is behind, I think, your tab
22. Exhibit 5828, Doc ID CTH.3111.0017.9701.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Now, with luck, that should be an email chain from the 6th of January 2017 that
you have?
MR GLADMAN: Yes. I've got it.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And the email chain commences with an email from
Mr Menzies-McVey to yourself on that date; correct?
MR GLADMAN: Yes. Correct.
MR SCOTT: And it opens with:
Mark, Sue Kruse would like us to develop as a top priority next week a paper on the
Department's current practice of averaging income for the purposes of calculating payments
under the social security law.
Do you see that?
MR GLADMAN: I do.
MR SCOTT: Thank you.

This paper should look at the legislative basis for this practice for each payment and identify
the circumstances where it is permissible for the Department to assume, in the absence of
other evidence, that income over a period has been earned pro rata over the period.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: You now understand - - -
MR GLADMAN: Sorry. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Did you understand then that to be a reference to the use made by the
Department at that stage of a practice of income averaging ATO data to calculate amounts of
income earned by a social security recipient in each fortnight?
MR GLADMAN: At that point in time, I had very little understanding or background in the
issue of income averaging.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
MR GLADMAN: I could go further.
MR SCOTT: Sure, please.
MR GLADMAN: So I had - I didn't have a background in social security law, and the first time
that I became aware of the - that there was an issue with income averaging - or a new - or
the first time I became aware of what we now know as Robodebt was when Mr
Menzies-McVey sent me a request for dot points. He was going to - or he had come back
from a senior meeting and said there was something hitting the media, could I provide some
dot points on income averaging. So I would have done some investigations, tried to work
out - because I didn't know what that was, tried to get some dot points. And then the next
time I would have come across it would have been with this request. I don't recall whether - I
recall a conversation with him about the request, but I don't recall whether the email came
first and then there was a conversation or the conversation and then the email.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Did you - would this be right: the dot points – sorry, I withdraw that. The
dot points that you've just referred to, is that something that's happened before this email?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So by the stage of this email, did you have at least a general sense that a
practice of income averaging was being used by the Department to calculate social security
recipients' fortnightly income?
MR GLADMAN: I don't recall exactly the extent of my knowledge. I knew there was
something hitting the media, that there were letters going out that people were concerned
about. And I - if I put some dot points together, then I must have drawn them from

conversation or Social Security Guide or something. So I must have had some knowledge, but
I think it was probably a fairly low level - it would have been a very low level of knowledge.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Well, your response to Mr Menzies-McVey, who was acting - he was Acting
Chief Counsel at that stage; correct?
MR GLADMAN: He was.
MR SCOTT: The substantive Chief Counsel was Ms Musolino?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Who was on leave at the time?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So your response to Mr Menzies-McVey's email was to indicate that you
would do as he had requested?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And based on Mr Menzies-McVey's email, did you understand that, effectively,
the product of the work that had been requested would be a legal advice?
MR GLADMAN: I had - not exactly. I had had a conversation with him. As I said, I'm not sure
whether it was before the email or after. And he had set out the circumstances in which this
question was coming up. And he had said that there had been a meeting, the media
inquiries - or the issues that were hitting the media had been raised. He said there had been
a conversation with Mr Britton. I don't recall whether he was at the meeting, or it was a
telephone conversation. And he had - Mr Britton had said, "Get the lawyers to explain how
we income" - well, I'm not sure if they used the word "income averaging", but explain what
we are doing, how we are doing it. So my understanding was, at least in the first instance, it
was an explanation of how it is that the Department is able to average income.
MR SCOTT: An explanation in the form of a legal advice or something else?
MR GLADMAN: I'm having some - I have read the - in preparing my Statement, I've gone
back, and I saw his request for advice, which talked about preparing a document that could
be shared with Ombudsman and other stakeholders. But I don't know how conscious I was at
that time that it might have a broader circulation. I probably was thinking of it, at least in the
first instance, being in the form of a legal advice.
MR SCOTT: Okay. But the document that - and we will get to it shortly, but you've reviewed
the draft documents that were prepared in response to this request in preparation for your
evidence today?

MR SCOTT: And the form of the document that was prepared in draft was originally in the
form of a draft legal advice?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And is that consistent with what you have just said, which you think that
you were probably thinking, at least in the first instance, of it being in the form of a legal
advice?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And you've mentioned that you had a limited understanding of the
program as at this date, the 6th of January. For the purpose of the work for the preparation
of the document in response to this request, did you subsequently gain a more detailed
understanding of the program?
MR GLADMAN: I've gained some more understanding at various points in processes over the
last four, five years. So I recall reading - I would describe myself as an interested observer
after I finished acting, because I had some involvement in it. So when - sorry, some
involvement in this - in advising on the Robodebt. So when the Ombudsman's reports came
out - - -
MR SCOTT: Can I just focus on - the intention of my question - and I apologise if it was
imprecise - was the development of your understanding of the program following this
request, up to the preparation of the first draft advice document. Did you - - -
MR GLADMAN: My apologies. I thought you were talking about my Statement for the
Commission.
MR SCOTT: Sure.
MR GLADMAN: Sorry. Can you just repeat it so I don't confuse the question.
MR SCOTT: Sure. So following this request from Mr Menzies-McVey - - -
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: - - - over the course of the work to prepare the document in response to this
request, did you then gain a more detailed understanding of the - of the program?
MR GLADMAN: No, I would not describe having a detailed understanding of the program.
MR SCOTT: But more detailed compared to what your understanding was at the stage that
you - of the receipt of this request?

MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. Did you have assistance from anybody within the Legal Services
Division for the purpose of preparing the document in response to this request?
MR GLADMAN: The document that's described as the averaging advice?
MR SCOTT: Yes.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Who did you get assistance from?
MR GLADMAN: John Barnett.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And what was the nature of the assistance that he provided?
MR GLADMAN: I initially referred the request to him, and then Mr Barnett did a first draft.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
COMMISSIONER: Do you happen to know where Mr Barnett is now?
MR GLADMAN: I believe - he lives in Tasmania. And - - -
COMMISSIONER: Any more detail than that?
MR GLADMAN: And retired, but I don't - I don't have his residential address or anything like
that.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Thank you. Do you know how he could be contacted? We have had a
little difficulty.
MR GLADMAN: I may have his - an old telephone number. I don't know. I could check.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. If you wouldn't mind, that would help.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Now, Mr Gladman, you mentioned at paragraph 21 of your first Statement that
you have been shown an email which would suggest that you attended a meeting with
Ms Carmody on the 9th of January 2017.
MR GLADMAN: Correct.

MR SCOTT: By that stage, that is, the 9th of January 2017, what role was Ms Carmody
occupying?
MR GLADMAN: Acting Chief Counsel.
MR SCOTT: The role that Mr Menzies-McVey had been acting in at the stage of the 6 January
2017 email?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And she had taken over the role of Acting Chief Counsel on the 9th of
January?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. Now, can I just ask that you be shown, please, what I think is
behind your tab 31, Mr Gladman, which is Doc ID MGL.0001.0001.0010. That should be
Exhibit 5836. Do you have that there, Mr Gladman?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Now, that would seem to be, would you agree, a calendar appointment
sent to you from Sue Gough with the subject ‘Briefing’ to occur on the 9th of January 2017,
and the time for the appointment is 4:30 am?
MR GLADMAN: Yes. That must be incorrect.
MR SCOTT: Right. Okay. So there was no meeting in the Chief Counsel's office at 4:30 am on
that date?
MR GLADMAN: No.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So there was only one meeting on that date?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: You think at 3:30 pm in the afternoon?
MR GLADMAN: I believe so.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
MR GLADMAN: From my examination of the documents.
MR SCOTT: Would it be unusual to be meeting with someone in your area at the time at 4:30
in the morning?

MR GLADMAN: Extremely.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, could I just interject by way of assistance. We will have
that document rechecked. One of the people assisting the Commission from AGS is in Perth,
and it may be that the way the document has been produced to the Commission picks up
their timeframe as opposed to - - -
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you for that.
MR SCOTT: I'm indebted to my learned friend. The next document I will seek to show you,
Mr Gladman, should be behind your tab 38, Exhibit 5843, Doc ID CTH.3113.0004.6850. Now,
do you agree with me that this is an email chain - so, firstly, do you have that document,
Mr Gladman?
MR GLADMAN: Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Do you agree with me this is an email chain that commences on the second
page with the email from Mr Menzies-McVey that we were just discussing before?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And then you inquire of Ms Carmody on the 9th of January at 9:30 am
whether she would like to see the draft before it is provided to Sue?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Sue being Sue Kruse?
MR GLADMAN: Kruse, yes.
MR SCOTT: And then Ms Carmody says:
Yes, please. And let's chat about it once I've had a look.
And thanks you. Do you see that top at the top of that page?
MR GLADMAN: Yes. I do.
MR SCOTT: And then on the first page - the first email in the chain on that page is from
yourself at 10:38 am. You thank Ms Carmody. You note:
Mr Barnett is working on this today.
You say:

I wouldn't expect that we will have anything for you to look at until tomorrow, but we will try
to get you something as soon as possible.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And then her email at 11.04 in the morning that day is in response:
Thanks, Mark. I understand this kept you all very busy late last week.
Do you see that?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Can you assist us from your recollection as to what she meant by those words, "I
understand this kept you all very busy late last week"?
MR GLADMAN: No. No, I don't recall.
MR SCOTT: Well, do you recall the work that followed Mr Menzies-McVey's email on the 6th
of January 2017 to implement the request that he made in that email involved a substantial
amount of work?
MR GLADMAN: Sorry, could you repeat the question?
MR SCOTT: Do you recall that the - implementing Mr Menzies-McVey's request in his 6
January 2017 email involved a substantial amount of work?
MR GLADMAN: It would, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. In circumstances where he had indicated that it was a top priority request?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And then in Ms Carmody's email, she notes that she had a handover from
Paul, Paul being Mr Menzies-McVey?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Okay. But then says:
I would like a briefing from you too, please. Can we chat about it today, perhaps this
afternoon if you have some time.
MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And then there's reference to the time for the meeting later in the chain.

MR GLADMAN: Correct.
MR SCOTT: But do you think it was at 3:30 instead?
MR GLADMAN: I think so, from my examination of the documents. It looks like it might have
been pushed back.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Do you have a recollection of what was discussed at that meeting on the
9th of January with Ms Carmody?
MR GLADMAN: No. I have a recollection of a particular meeting with Ms Carmody, which I
think, when I look at the document, is more likely to have occurred on the 10th rather than
the 9th, which means I have no - I have no recollection in those circumstances of what we
discussed on the 9th.
MR SCOTT: What makes you think you had a meeting with Ms Carmody - so I will take it in
steps. Do you - do you accept that there was a meeting on the 9th of January 2017 with
Ms Carmody?
MR GLADMAN: I have no reason to doubt the documents.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And - but then you believe that there was a further meeting on the 10th of
January 2017?
MR GLADMAN: I believe so.
MR SCOTT: By which time you had seen drafts of the averaging advice?
MR GLADMAN: I believe - yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I now want to ask you to be shown, Mr Gladman, the document behind
your tab 39, which is Doc ID CTH.3113.0004.7075, Exhibit 5844. Do you see that? Do you see
that, Mr Gladman?
MR GLADMAN: Yes. I do.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Do you agree with me that it refers to an attached draft advice for
Ms Carmody's consideration?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And then the attachment is behind your tab 40, Exhibit 5845, Doc ID
CTH.3113.0004.7076. Do you have that?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.

MR SCOTT: Do you agree with me that that is the draft advice as it - in its then state of
development at 3:57 pm on the 10th of January 2017?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Paragraph 3 of that draft - - -
MR GLADMAN: Sorry, can you point me to the tab again? I was still on the covering email.
MR SCOTT: My apologies. Tab 40.
MR GLADMAN: Tab 40.
MR SCOTT: Yes.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: I just want to ask you firstly about paragraph 3.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you see the words:
We think there are some reasonable arguments that could be made to support the process
involving the use of information received from the ATO.
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: I just want you to mentally note those words "we think there are some
reasonable arguments that could be made".
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: I am going to ask you about those words shortly.
MR GLADMAN: Sure.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And then paragraph 4 has these words:
Given the complexity of the legislation and the significance of this issue for the Department, it
may be prudent to obtain external legal advice on this matter.
Do you see that?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.

MR SCOTT: Now, what I want to do, Mr Gladman, is ask you about paragraph 24 of your first
Statement.
MR GLADMAN: Yes. Sorry. Yes, I've got the first Statement.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Now, is that paragraph where you describe what you recall occurred
at the meeting with Ms Carmody on the 10th of January 2017?
MR GLADMAN: I believe it would have occurred on the 10th, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And can you just describe for us what your recollection is of what occurred
on that date at that meeting?
MR GLADMAN: My recollection is I had received the first draft advice from Mr Barnett. I had
started a process of sort of editing it, moving things around, trying to make things clearer.
And I got to a point where - I was - I felt that we were trying to, in the first instance, identify
arguments that would support what the Department and the government was doing. And I
got to a point where I felt that the arguments didn't support a conclusion that there are
reasonable - there was a reasonable basis based on the material before me.
MR SCOTT: Didn't support that there was a reasonable basis based on the material before
you?
MR GLADMAN: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Basis for what?
MR GLADMAN: I didn't - at that point in time, I didn't feel that I could reach the conclusion
that there were reasonable arguments to support income averaging.
MR SCOTT: Right.
MR GLADMAN: But I also felt that there was a number of matters that I needed to explore
further.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Just for the non-lawyers in the room and watching this, what is - when a
lawyer forms a view that there are not reasonable arguments to support averaging, what
does that mean in a practical sense?
MR GLADMAN: That the stronger arguments are that you can't average.
MR SCOTT: And that - is this right: that if the matter were to be determined by a court, the
court would more likely find that you can't - that is, the Department couldn't lawfully
averaging?
MR GLADMAN: Correct.

MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. So I cut you off, I think, Mr Gladman. You say you had formed
that view. And what else did you - what other aspects did you turn your mind to?
MR GLADMAN: I - I had two levels of concern when I was looking at the draft advice. So the
position I thought we were trying to reach, at least in the first instance if we could, was to
identify reasonable arguments to support what the Department was doing. I had two levels
of concerns: one was a factual concern; and one was more of a legal concern about the
potential arguments.
MR SCOTT: What was the factual concern?
MR GLADMAN: We had limited detail on what Robodebt involved, just really those dot
points that were in the draft advice. The more I looked at our arguments, the more I started
to question whether that was really an accurate description of what the Department was
trying to achieve in - in whatever processes it was doing. So I remember being concerned - I
remember I kept thinking, well, how would this apply to a student, for instance, because
students often work full-time over a summer break and a little bit in other times, and then
maybe periods of the year they don't work at all. How does - how would averaging work
mathematically?
And so I was - I started to question - myself, anyway, I started to think there must be more to
this because that seems like an obvious problem. People must have addressed this in the
design. I also was starting to think - or at least identify as an area of investigation whether
the implementation and the design of the Scheme were in alignment, that is,
whether - whether there had been a decision to do something a little bit different
to - whether there was an error in design or whether there was an error in implementation. I
wasn't sure. I wanted to investigate that.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And you mentioned also a legal concern. Is that the concern you described
earlier about there not being strong arguments in support of averaging?
MR GLADMAN: My - at this stage, I felt that I was in a fact-finding role. And the legal concern
was I was aware that there had been a practice of averaging as a last resort, but I didn't
understand what the legal argument is that allows you to average even in a last resort. And
so I wanted to understand whether - I wanted to look at previous AGS - sorry, previous AAT
decisions if they had considered it, if there was previous Department of Social Services legal
advice or DHS legal advice. Because I thought if it's a long-standing practice, then these
questions must have come up before and someone must have considered it. So I wanted
to - I wanted to examine that.
MR SCOTT: What was the basis of your understanding that averaging had been done
historically as a last resort?
MR GLADMAN: The Social Security Guide, I think.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And what did you understand averaging as a last resort to mean?

MR GLADMAN: After they have - after inquiries have been made to try to get material and
they have exhausted all of their avenues of inquiry.
MR SCOTT: Inquiries with whom?
MR GLADMAN: The recipients and employers. I'm not sure if - if they went further.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Did you reach any conclusions as to what recommendation should be
made for the purpose of your discussion with Ms Kruse on the 10th of January 2017?
MR GLADMAN: The - the purpose of my meeting was to make a recommendation to her.
MR SCOTT: What was the recommendation that you had a purpose of making?
MR GLADMAN: That rather than do an internal advice, we go straight to getting external
advice.
MR SCOTT: And why did you think that should be done?
MR GLADMAN: I thought that - a number of - a number of reasons. In - in the first instance, I
wanted to put in place a process where we could start to do some of this fact-finding that I
was - or this investigation that I was referring to. So a process to understand what is it the
Department was trying to achieve? What was its implementation? Had they - what
consideration had been given to some kinds of benefits? Are they - were they intended to be
excluded from this? What advice had been previously given? And what options might there
be to effectively re-engineer the processes? So that's - that, I thought, would involve quite a
bit of work. And one of the situations where we would often get external advice is when you
just don't have the capacity to - someone in-house just hasn't got the time to, say, go offline
and just work on that. That was one reason.
So I thought they would put in place - essentially a process by which the in-house lawyers
could work with the clients and with AGS. They could identify question, identify background,
and there would be a way of examining issues. And it would probably slow things down a
little bit, because we had been asked to do it in two days. This would sort of allow it to be a
little bit more considered. The - I thought - often we get legal advice externally because of
expertise. And the - I thought some of the judgment calls that might be involved in working
out to what extent can you use ATO information, how far can we use it, would require some
judgment calls, which you would want people who have good background in admin law and
government decision-making. And the third reason was to provide a level of arm's length
consideration or objectivity or something along those lines.
MR SCOTT: That is, arm's length from the Department?
MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And greater objectivity of the advice - - -

MR GLADMAN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: - - - than if it had been provided in-house?
MR GLADMAN: At the least, it gives people assurance that it's being looked at by - it's being
objectively considered because it is being considered by someone external to the
Department.
MR SCOTT: That process of fact-finding that you are describing, am I right in understanding
